question.text: What lights must come on with the brakes or turn signals, and how far must they be visible in daylight?

answer.text: Every motor vehicle built since one thousand nine hundred fifty-five must have red or amber lights that come on with the brakes or turn signals, visible for at least one hundred feet in normal daylight.

teaching.text: Vehicles built since nineteen fifty-five need red or amber brake and turn lights visible for one hundred feet in daylight. Remember: red or amber, one hundred feet.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Every motor vehicle built since one thousand nine hundred fifty-five must have red or amber lights that come on with the brakes or turn signals, visible for at least one hundred feet in normal daylight.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: red or amber, one hundred feet

question.text: Must brake and turn lights be part of the taillights?

answer.text: Those brake and turn lights may be built into the taillights or mounted separately; either arrangement is allowed.

teaching.text: Those lights may be part of the taillights or mounted on their own. Remember: combined or separate is fine.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Those brake and turn lights may be built into the taillights or mounted separately; either arrangement is allowed.

question.text: What two things does the handbook say about brake and turn lights?

answer.text: Brake and turn lights must show for at least one hundred feet in daylight, and they may either share the taillight housing or be mounted on their own.

teaching.text: The rule is the color and the one hundred foot daylight visibility, with either mounting allowed. Remember: visible far, mounted either way.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Brake and turn lights must show for at least one hundred feet in daylight, and they may either share the taillight housing or be mounted on their own.

question.text: Why should light lenses stay clean and working?

answer.text: Keep light lenses clean and the lights working, because hand signals are hard for other drivers to see after dark.

teaching.text: Keep lenses clean and lights working, since hand signals are hard to see after dark. Remember: hand signals vanish after dark.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep light lenses clean and the lights working, because hand signals are hard for other drivers to see after dark.

question.text: What should the inside mirror and the side mirrors show?

answer.text: Check and set the mirrors before driving: the inside mirror shows straight behind, and the side mirrors show the left and right rear while just barely showing the car's own side.

teaching.text: Set mirrors before driving: inside for straight behind, sides for the rear while barely showing your own car. Remember: set mirrors before driving.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Check and set the mirrors before driving: the inside mirror shows straight behind, and the side mirrors show the left and right rear while just barely showing the car's own side.

question.text: What must the brakes on any vehicle using a public road be able to do?

answer.text: Any motor vehicle on a public road must have brakes able to control it, stop it and hold it in place.

teaching.text: Brakes must be able to control, stop and hold the vehicle. Remember: control, stop, hold.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Any motor vehicle on a public road must have brakes able to control it, stop it and hold it in place.

question.text: How many separate ways of applying the brakes should factory brakes provide?

answer.text: Factory brakes should be kept in good condition and provide two separate ways of applying the brakes.

teaching.text: Factory brakes should be kept in good condition with two separate ways to apply them. Remember: two ways to brake.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Factory brakes should be kept in good condition and provide two separate ways of applying the brakes.

question.text: How high should a fully pressed brake pedal stay above the floor?

answer.text: When pressed all the way, the brake pedal should stay at least one-third of its original distance above the floor; if not, have the brakes checked and repaired.

teaching.text: A fully pressed pedal should stay at least a third of its travel above the floor, or get the brakes checked. Remember: a third above the floor.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When pressed all the way, the brake pedal should stay at least one-third of its original distance above the floor; if not, have the brakes checked and repaired.

question.text: What does a slowly sinking brake pedal mean?

answer.text: A brake pedal that slowly sinks under steady foot pressure means the hydraulic system needs checking, and squeaking brakes should also be inspected.

teaching.text: A pedal that sinks under steady pressure means the hydraulics need checking, and squeaks need inspection too. Remember: sinking pedal, check hydraulics.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A brake pedal that slowly sinks under steady foot pressure means the hydraulic system needs checking, and squeaking brakes should also be inspected.

question.text: What three things do anti-lock brakes help with?

answer.text: Anti-lock brakes (ABS) help with stability against spin-outs, with steering where you intend, and with stopping distance.

teaching.text: ABS helps with stability against spin-outs, steering where you intend, and stopping distance. Remember: stability, steering, stopping.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Anti-lock brakes (ABS) help with stability against spin-outs, with steering where you intend, and with stopping distance.

question.text: How should you brake in a car with anti-lock brakes?

answer.text: With ABS, brake hard and hold firm, steady pressure; pumping the pedal or easing off reduces how well ABS works.

teaching.text: With ABS, brake hard and hold steady, since pumping or easing off reduces how well it works. Remember: press hard and hold.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: With ABS, brake hard and hold firm, steady pressure; pumping the pedal or easing off reduces how well ABS works.

question.text: Should you pump the pedal when braking with ABS?

answer.text: With anti-lock brakes you press hard and hold steady, which is the opposite of pumping the pedal.

teaching.text: Anti-lock brakes call for firm, steady pressure, the opposite of pumping. Remember: hold, do not pump.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: With anti-lock brakes you press hard and hold steady, which is the opposite of pumping the pedal.

question.text: What should you never leave in an unattended vehicle?

answer.text: To discourage theft, never leave the key in the ignition of a vehicle you are not attending.

teaching.text: Never leave the key in the ignition of a vehicle you are not attending. Remember: take your keys.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To discourage theft, never leave the key in the ignition of a vehicle you are not attending.

question.text: When is a tire legally unsafe?

answer.text: A tire is legally unsafe if a cut, crack or wear exposes the cord, if it shows tread separation or chunking, or if tread depth is under one or sixteen inch.

teaching.text: Exposed cord, tread separation or chunking, or tread under one-sixteenth of an inch makes a tire legally unsafe. Remember: exposed cord or thin tread.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A tire is legally unsafe if a cut, crack or wear exposes the cord, if it shows tread separation or chunking, or if tread depth is under one or sixteen inch.

question.text: What happens to under-inflated and over-inflated tires?

answer.text: Under-inflated tires wear out faster and are more likely to blow out, while over-inflated tires lose traction and wear down the center of the tread.

teaching.text: Low pressure means faster wear and blowout risk, while high pressure means less traction and center wear. Remember: low wears fast, high slips.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Under-inflated tires wear out faster and are more likely to blow out, while over-inflated tires lose traction and wear down the center of the tread.

question.text: How do the problems of under-inflated and over-inflated tires differ?

answer.text: Under-inflated tires wear fast and risk blowouts, while over-inflated tires lose grip and wear the middle of the tread.

teaching.text: Under-inflation brings wear and blowouts, while over-inflation brings lost grip and center wear. Remember: under blows out, over slips.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Under-inflated tires wear fast and risk blowouts, while over-inflated tires lose grip and wear the middle of the tread.

question.text: Which limits apply to tire tread depth and brake pedal height?

answer.text: A tire becomes unsafe below one or sixteen inch of tread, while the brake pedal must stay at least one-third of its travel above the floor.

teaching.text: The tread limit is one-sixteenth of an inch, and the pressed pedal must stay a third above the floor. Remember: thin tread, low pedal.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A tire becomes unsafe below one or sixteen inch of tread, while the brake pedal must stay at least one-third of its travel above the floor.

question.text: How often should you check tire pressure, and when?

answer.text: Check tire air pressure at least once a month, preferably while the tires are cool, following the manufacturer's recommended pressure.

teaching.text: Check pressure at least monthly, ideally on cool tires, to the manufacturer's recommendation. Remember: monthly, while tires are cool.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Check tire air pressure at least once a month, preferably while the tires are cool, following the manufacturer's recommended pressure.

question.text: Which vehicles may carry emergency lights or sirens?

answer.text: Only law enforcement and emergency vehicles are permitted to carry emergency lights or sirens.

teaching.text: Only law enforcement and emergency vehicles may carry emergency lights or sirens. Remember: sirens for responders only.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Only law enforcement and emergency vehicles are permitted to carry emergency lights or sirens.

question.text: How far away must a horn be heard, and what sound is not allowed?

answer.text: Every licensed motor vehicle needs a working horn that can be heard from at least two hundred feet without an unreasonably loud or harsh sound.

teaching.text: A horn must be heard from two hundred feet without being unreasonably loud or harsh. Remember: heard at two hundred feet.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Every licensed motor vehicle needs a working horn that can be heard from at least two hundred feet without an unreasonably loud or harsh sound.

question.text: When should you use the horn?

answer.text: Use the horn only as a reasonable warning, never needlessly, and get a failed horn fixed right away.

teaching.text: Use the horn only as a reasonable warning, and fix a failed horn right away. Remember: horn for warnings only.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use the horn only as a reasonable warning, never needlessly, and get a failed horn fixed right away.

question.text: What two limits apply to a vehicle horn?

answer.text: The horn must be heard from at least two hundred feet, yet it must not give an unreasonably loud or harsh sound, so both limits apply at once.

teaching.text: The horn needs enough volume for two hundred feet but must not be harsh. Remember: loud enough, never harsh.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The horn must be heard from at least two hundred feet, yet it must not give an unreasonably loud or harsh sound, so both limits apply at once.

question.text: What does a working muffler do?

answer.text: Every motor vehicle must have a working muffler, which reduces smoke and excess noise.

teaching.text: Every vehicle needs a working muffler, which cuts smoke and excess noise. Remember: muffler cuts smoke and noise.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Every motor vehicle must have a working muffler, which reduces smoke and excess noise.

question.text: What can an exhaust leak cause, and what does the handbook suggest?

answer.text: An exhaust leak can let carbon monoxide into the cabin, which can cause drowsiness, unconsciousness or death, so the handbook suggests driving with a window open about one inch.

teaching.text: An exhaust leak can let carbon monoxide inside, so the handbook suggests a window open about an inch. Remember: leaks bring carbon monoxide.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: An exhaust leak can let carbon monoxide into the cabin, which can cause drowsiness, unconsciousness or death, so the handbook suggests driving with a window open about one inch.

question.text: What signs point to a suspension problem?

answer.text: Swaying, leaning hard in turns or constant bouncing can signal a suspension problem, which should be inspected and fixed at once because it can cause loss of control.

teaching.text: Swaying, hard leaning or constant bouncing can mean a suspension problem that needs fixing at once. Remember: sway, lean, bounce.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Swaying, leaning hard in turns or constant bouncing can signal a suspension problem, which should be inspected and fixed at once because it can cause loss of control.

question.text: What do emergency flashers do, and who may use them?

answer.text: The emergency flashers blink all four turn signals and may be used by any vehicle to warn of danger or show it is stopped or disabled.

teaching.text: Flashers blink all four turn signals, and any vehicle may use them to warn or to show it is stopped. Remember: flashers for any vehicle.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The emergency flashers blink all four turn signals and may be used by any vehicle to warn of danger or show it is stopped or disabled.

question.text: How do hazard flashers differ from emergency lights and sirens?

answer.text: Hazard flashers may be used by any vehicle, while emergency lights and sirens are reserved for law enforcement and emergency vehicles.

teaching.text: Any vehicle may use flashers, but emergency lights and sirens are reserved. Remember: flashers for all, sirens reserved.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hazard flashers may be used by any vehicle, while emergency lights and sirens are reserved for law enforcement and emergency vehicles.

question.text: How much can each five miles per hour above sixty add to fuel cost?

answer.text: For fuel economy, each five miles per hour driven above sixty miles per hour can add up to about thirty cents per gallon in cost.

teaching.text: Each five miles per hour above sixty can add up to about thirty cents per gallon. Remember: speed costs fuel.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For fuel economy, each five miles per hour driven above sixty miles per hour can add up to about thirty cents per gallon in cost.

question.text: How much can sudden starts and hard stops raise fuel use?

answer.text: Sudden starts and hard stops can raise fuel use by as much as forty percent.

teaching.text: Sudden starts and hard stops can raise fuel use by as much as forty percent. Remember: smooth driving saves fuel.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Sudden starts and hard stops can raise fuel use by as much as forty percent.

question.text: When should you turn off the engine, and when use windows versus air conditioning?

answer.text: To save fuel, switch off the engine if you will wait more than a couple of minutes, and open the windows below forty miles per hour but use air conditioning above it.

teaching.text: Turn the engine off for waits over a couple of minutes, and use windows below forty and air conditioning above. Remember: idle off, windows slow.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To save fuel, switch off the engine if you will wait more than a couple of minutes, and open the windows below forty miles per hour but use air conditioning above it.

question.text: How do a clogged air filter and a loose fuel cap waste fuel?

answer.text: A clogged air filter can lower mileage by about ten percent, and a loose fuel cap can let up to thirty gallons of gas a year escape.

teaching.text: A clogged air filter can cut mileage about ten percent, and a loose cap can lose thirty gallons a year. Remember: clean filter, tight cap.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A clogged air filter can lower mileage by about ten percent, and a loose fuel cap can let up to thirty gallons of gas a year escape.

question.text: How far ahead should you look while driving?

answer.text: Good drivers look ten to fifteen seconds ahead, roughly one city block, to avoid last-second stops and lane changes.

teaching.text: Look ten to fifteen seconds ahead, about one city block, to avoid last-second moves. Remember: look a block ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Good drivers look ten to fifteen seconds ahead, roughly one city block, to avoid last-second stops and lane changes.

question.text: How often should you glance at your mirrors?

answer.text: Glance at the mirrors about every ten seconds to spot a vehicle following too closely, taking your eyes off the road only for an instant.

teaching.text: Glance at the mirrors about every ten seconds, only for an instant. Remember: mirrors every ten seconds.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Glance at the mirrors about every ten seconds to spot a vehicle following too closely, taking your eyes off the road only for an instant.

question.text: How do the look-ahead time and the mirror-check interval differ?

answer.text: Look ten to fifteen seconds ahead of the car, but check the mirrors about every ten seconds.

teaching.text: The look-ahead is ten to fifteen seconds, while mirror checks come about every ten seconds. Remember: ahead longer, mirrors often.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Look ten to fifteen seconds ahead of the car, but check the mirrors about every ten seconds.

question.text: When should you check behind you and your blind spots?

answer.text: Check behind you and your blind spots when changing lanes, backing, slowing down or going down a long hill.

teaching.text: Check behind and your blind spots when changing lanes, backing, slowing or going down a long hill. Remember: check behind before changes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Check behind you and your blind spots when changing lanes, backing, slowing down or going down a long hill.

question.text: Where are blind spots, and how do you check them?

answer.text: Blind spots are the areas near the left and right rear corners that mirrors cannot show, so turn your head and look over your shoulder before a lane change or turn.

teaching.text: Blind spots sit near the rear corners where mirrors cannot reach, so look over your shoulder. Remember: look over your shoulder.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Blind spots are the areas near the left and right rear corners that mirrors cannot show, so turn your head and look over your shoulder before a lane change or turn.

question.text: Can mirrors alone show the rear-corner blind spots?

answer.text: Mirrors show the scene behind, but the rear-corner blind spots need a quick look over the shoulder.

teaching.text: Mirrors show behind, but the rear corners need a shoulder check. Remember: mirrors miss the corners.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Mirrors show the scene behind, but the rear-corner blind spots need a quick look over the shoulder.

question.text: What should you do when glare or parked cars block your view?

answer.text: Glare, a dirty windshield, cars parked near an intersection, bushes or buildings can also block your view; ease forward until you can see clearly.

teaching.text: When glare, parked cars, bushes or buildings block your view, ease forward until you can see. Remember: ease forward to see.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Glare, a dirty windshield, cars parked near an intersection, bushes or buildings can also block your view; ease forward until you can see clearly.

question.text: When should you signal?

answer.text: Signal whenever you plan to slow, stop, turn, change lanes or leave the curb, even with no one in sight, but first confirm the move is safe.

teaching.text: Signal every slow, stop, turn, lane change or curb exit, even with no one around, after checking it is safe. Remember: signal every move.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Signal whenever you plan to slow, stop, turn, change lanes or leave the curb, even with no one in sight, but first confirm the move is safe.

question.text: What can make turn signal lights hard to see?

answer.text: Turn-signal lights legally replace hand signals, but low morning or evening sun on the lenses can make it hard to tell whether they are flashing.

teaching.text: Signal lights legally replace hand signals, but low sun can hide whether they are flashing. Remember: low sun hides signals.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Turn-signal lights legally replace hand signals, but low morning or evening sun on the lenses can make it hard to tell whether they are flashing.

question.text: How far before a turn or stop must you signal, and how far at higher speed limits?

answer.text: Signal for at least the last one hundred feet before turning or stopping, and at least the last two hundred feet before a turn when the speed limit is forty-five miles per hour or higher.

teaching.text: Signal at least one hundred feet before turning or stopping, and two hundred feet before a turn at forty-five or more. Remember: one hundred, or two hundred.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Signal for at least the last one hundred feet before turning or stopping, and at least the last two hundred feet before a turn when the speed limit is forty-five miles per hour or higher.

question.text: When does the signaling distance double to two hundred feet?

answer.text: Signal at least one hundred feet before a turn or stop in general, and at least two hundred feet before a turn where the limit is forty-five miles per hour or more.

teaching.text: The general distance is one hundred feet, and two hundred feet for turns where the limit is forty-five or more. Remember: faster roads, signal earlier.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Signal at least one hundred feet before a turn or stop in general, and at least two hundred feet before a turn where the limit is forty-five miles per hour or more.

question.text: What is the hand signal for a left turn?

answer.text: Hand signals use the left arm out the driver's window: arm straight out with finger pointing for a left turn.

teaching.text: For a left turn, hold the left arm straight out with the finger pointing. Remember: arm straight out, left.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hand signals use the left arm out the driver's window: arm straight out with finger pointing for a left turn.

question.text: What is the hand signal for a right turn?

answer.text: For a right turn by hand, hold the arm out with the forearm and hand raised and the palm forward.

teaching.text: For a right turn, hold the arm out with the forearm and hand raised and the palm forward. Remember: forearm up, right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For a right turn by hand, hold the arm out with the forearm and hand raised and the palm forward.

question.text: What is the hand signal for slowing or stopping?

answer.text: To signal slowing or stopping by hand, point the arm and hand downward with the palm facing back.

teaching.text: To slow or stop, point the arm and hand down with the palm facing back. Remember: arm down, stopping.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To signal slowing or stopping by hand, point the arm and hand downward with the palm facing back.

question.text: What do the three hand signals mean?

answer.text: Arm straight out means a left turn, forearm up means a right turn, and arm pointed down means slowing or stopping.

teaching.text: Straight out for left, raised for right, and down for slowing or stopping. Remember: out left, up right, down stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Arm straight out means a left turn, forearm up means a right turn, and arm pointed down means slowing or stopping.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: out left, up right, down stop

question.text: What should you do when a driver follows you too closely?

answer.text: If a driver follows too closely, change lanes and signal for that driver to pass; stay centered in your lane with space on both sides.

teaching.text: When tailgated, change lanes and signal the driver to pass, and stay centered with space on both sides. Remember: let tailgaters pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If a driver follows too closely, change lanes and signal for that driver to pass; stay centered in your lane with space on both sides.

question.text: Facing two unequal dangers, which one gets the most room?

answer.text: When facing two unavoidable dangers at once, give the most room to the one that is worst or most likely, such as a child on a bicycle rather than oncoming cars.

teaching.text: With two unavoidable dangers, give the most room to the worst or most likely, like a child on a bicycle. Remember: room for the worst danger.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When facing two unavoidable dangers at once, give the most room to the one that is worst or most likely, such as a child on a bicycle rather than oncoming cars.

question.text: What should you do when two dangers are equally serious?

answer.text: If two dangers are equally serious, such as oncoming traffic and parked cars, stop and let the oncoming vehicles pass before going on.

teaching.text: With two equally serious dangers, stop and let oncoming vehicles pass first. Remember: stop, let oncoming pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If two dangers are equally serious, such as oncoming traffic and parked cars, stop and let the oncoming vehicles pass before going on.

question.text: How does handling unequal dangers differ from handling equal dangers?

answer.text: With unequal dangers give more room to the most likely one, but with equal dangers stop and let oncoming traffic go by.

teaching.text: Unequal dangers mean more room for the worse one, and equal dangers mean stopping for oncoming traffic. Remember: unequal, give room; equal, stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: With unequal dangers give more room to the most likely one, but with equal dangers stop and let oncoming traffic go by.

recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of tires. Exposed cord, separation or very thin tread makes a tire unsafe. Check pressure monthly while tires are cool. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.
